title: Governance Adequacy and the Preservation of Institutional Authority in Distributed Intelligent Systems
content: An intelligent system can produce a correct recommendation while making an unauthorized commitment. This article argues that governing such systems requires representations that preserve the distinctions on which authorization, accountability, and institutional revision depend. Governance adequacy is defined relative to a class of runs and a declared family of governance predicates. A representation is adequate when runs it identifies agree on those predicates. A factorization result establishes the criterion, while a counterexample shows why identical activity logs can conceal different authority histories. The analysis distinguishes retrospective adequacy from the information available to an enforcing component and separates institutional authorization from moral legitimacy. Burgin’s General Theory of Information and structural approaches to computation provide a vocabulary for representing governing relations without implying computational superiority. A proposed architecture separates advice, delegated adjudication, commitment enforcement, and accountable amendment. A conditional invariant identifies the assumptions needed to preserve authorization through execution and recovery. Analytical examples examine password resets, queued healthcare approvals, and replacement of executors with outstanding duties. Biological self-maintenance is treated as a limited analogy rather than a source of political authority. The central conclusion is that continuity should preserve justified commitments and unresolved obligations, not merely executable state.
